t:
For environmental reviews and approvals carried out on projects funded under title 23, United States Code, the Comptroller General of the United States shall—
    (1) review State laws and procedures for conducting environmental reviews with regard to such projects and identify the States that have environmental laws that provide environmental protections and opportunities for public involvement that are equivalent to those provided by Federal environmental laws; 
    (2) determine the frequency and cost of environmental reviews carried out at the Federal level that are duplicative of State reviews that provide equivalent environmental protections and opportunities for public involvement; and 
    (3) not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act, submit to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Environment and Public Works of the Senate a report that describes the results of the review and determination made under this section.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to "opportunities for public involvement" signal participation, but that phrase only describes what the Comptroller General must study in State laws. The section directs a GAO review and a report to congressional committees, all of which stays inside the federal government. No outside party is consulted, heard, or given a right to challenge any federal decision.
fable.s: submit to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Environment and Public Works of the Senate a report that describes the results of the review and determination made under this section

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Comptroller General to conduct a study and submit a report to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation by outside parties. Although the text mentions 'opportunities for public involvement' in state laws, the section itself does not require or establish any such participation; it only mandates a review of existing state procedures.
qwen_block.s: submit to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Environment and Public Works of the Senate a report that describes the results of the review and determination made under this section.

opus.w: The Comptroller General only reviews State laws and reports the results to House and Senate committees, which is a study and report that stays entirely inside the federal government. "Public involvement" is a topic of the review, not a process this section creates for outside parties to take part in a federal decision. No comment period, hearing, advisory body, outside consultation or right to sue is established.
opus.s: identify the States that have environmental laws that provide environmental protections and opportunities for public involvement that are equivalent to those provided by Federal environmental laws
opus.b: The tempting reading is "Yes", because the section twice mentions "opportunities for public involvement." But that phrase only describes what the Comptroller General must study: whether State environmental laws give the public chances to be involved. The section does not create any public comment period, hearing or consultation with outsiders before a federal decision. Its only output is a report to two congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government.

qwen_chat.w: This section requires the Comptroller General to conduct a study and submit a report to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is not participation. The section evaluates state laws regarding public involvement but does not itself create a mechanism for outside parties to participate in federal decision-making.
qwen_chat.s: submit to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Environment and Public Works of the Senate a report that describes the results of the review and determination made under this section.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Comptroller General is tasked with identifying states that provide "opportunities for public involvement," this section itself requires or facilitates public participation. However, the section only mandates a *study* and *report* by a federal official (the Comptroller General) to Congress. It does not establish a process for the public to participate in a federal decision, nor does it require the federal government to consult with the public. The "public involvement" mentioned is a characteristic of *state* laws being evaluated, not a federal participation mechanism being enacted.
